leaves.name: Linear Algebra
leaves.brief: A matrix is a machine that moves vectors, and linear algebra is learning to read it.
leaves.sentence: A matrix is a machine that moves vectors. Linear algebra is learning to read that machine: first by what it does to the grid, then by what it reaches and what it crushes, then by the directions it leaves alone.
leaves.teacher: Four parts. Part I builds with vectors (span, independence, basis, dot product) so that Part II can read a matrix as a machine described by its columns. Part II runs machine, product, composition, determinant, systems, inverse, elimination, and the four subspaces, in the order need before tool: systems are asked before the inverse answers them. Part III brings length and angle back for projection, least squares and orthonormal bases. Part IV reads the machine on its own axes and ends with SVD, where the shear that defeated eigenvectors gives in. Two house matrices, S and the shear H, recur from page 6 to page 20.

pages.title: Vectors
pages.brief: A vector is a size and a direction given together.
pages.seo_title: Vectors: size and direction, explained visually
pages.description: A vector is a size and a direction given together. Drag arrows, add and scale them, and predict where they land.
pages.idea: A vector is a size and a direction given together.

pages.title: Span
pages.brief: The span is every point you can reach by adding and scaling some arrows.
pages.forward: w = (−1, 1), the partner p on v's line, and a trail that refused to leave the line
pages.seo_title: Span: what two arrows can reach, visually
pages.description: The span of some arrows is every point you can reach by adding and scaling them. Paint it with two sliders, then predict what it covers.
pages.idea: The span of some arrows is every point you can reach by adding and scaling them.

pages.title: Linear independence
pages.brief: An arrow is independent when the others cannot reach it.
pages.forward: a test for redundancy without the word parallel

pages.title: Basis and coordinates
pages.brief: A basis is the smallest set of arrows that reaches everything.

pages.title: Dot product
pages.brief: The dot product is one number that says how much two arrows agree.

pages.title: Matrices as machines
pages.brief: A matrix is a machine that moves every arrow and keeps the grid straight.
pages.forward: the house matrices S and H

pages.title: Matrix times vector
pages.brief: Ax can be read as a recipe of columns or as dot products with rows.
pages.forward: the transpose, lightly, with a promise

pages.title: Composition
pages.brief: Two machines one after another make one machine, and the order matters.

pages.title: Determinant
pages.brief: The determinant is how much the machine stretches area.

pages.title: Systems Ax = b
pages.brief: A system asks which input the machine sends to b.
pages.forward: one, none or infinitely many, and why

pages.title: Inverse
pages.brief: The inverse is the machine that undoes A, when undoing is possible.
pages.forward: a crushed plane cannot be uncrushed

pages.title: Elimination
pages.brief: Elimination changes the equations without changing the answer.

pages.title: Column space, null space, rank
pages.brief: Rank counts what the machine reaches; the rest it crushes to zero.
pages.forward: eigenvectors live in a null space

pages.title: Projection onto a subspace
pages.brief: A projection is the closest point, and its error is perpendicular.

pages.title: Least squares
pages.brief: When no exact answer exists, least squares finds the nearest one.

pages.title: Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt
pages.brief: Orthonormal arrows are perpendicular and of length 1, so coordinates become dot products.
pages.forward: the inverse of a rotation is its transpose

pages.title: Eigenvectors
pages.brief: An eigenvector keeps its direction when the machine moves it.
pages.description: An eigenvector is a direction that a matrix only stretches. Drag the arrow, predict where it lands, then see why.
pages.idea: An eigenvector is a direction that a matrix only stretches.

pages.title: Change of basis and diagonalisation
pages.brief: Read the machine in its eigen-basis and it only stretches.

pages.title: Symmetric matrices
pages.brief: A symmetric machine stretches along perpendicular axes.

pages.title: SVD
pages.brief: Every machine is a rotation, a stretch and a rotation.

branches.title: Homogeneous coordinates
branches.brief: Translation is not a linear machine, so graphics adds one coordinate to make it one.

branches.title: Hill cipher
branches.brief: A cipher is a matrix that can be undone mod 26.

branches.title: Regression
branches.brief: Least squares on the fifteen is a regression line.

branches.title: PageRank
branches.brief: A search ranking is the eigenvector of a web graph.

branches.title: PCA
branches.brief: The covariance matrix of the fifteen is symmetric, and its eigenvectors point along the data.

glossary.def: A size and a direction given together; drawn as an arrow, written as a list of components.
Every point you can reach by adding and scaling some arrows.
An arrow the others cannot reach; only the zero recipe makes zero.
The smallest set of arrows that reaches everything.
One number that says how much two arrows agree; zero when they are perpendicular.
A machine that moves every arrow and keeps the grid straight; its columns say where the basis arrows land.
How much the machine stretches area; negative means a flip, zero means the plane collapses.
The question: which input does the machine send to b?
The machine that undoes A; it exists only when the determinant is not zero.
Row moves that change the equations without changing the answer.
The dimension of what the machine reaches.
The closest point in a subspace; its error is perpendicular.
The nearest reachable answer when no exact one exists.
An arrow that keeps its direction when the machine moves it.
The number λ that says how much a matrix stretches its eigenvector: Av = λv.
A matrix equal to its transpose; it stretches along perpendicular axes.

leaves.name: Functions
leaves.brief: A function is a machine: one input goes in, one output comes out.
leaves.sentence: A function is a machine that takes an input and returns one output; composition chains machines and an inverse runs one backwards.
leaves.why: The machine idea of the whole Linear Algebra leaf is born here, one leaf earlier, so composition and inverse become returns.

leaves.name: Trigonometry and the unit circle
leaves.brief: An angle is a place on the dial, and sine and cosine are its two shadows.
leaves.sentence: An angle is a position on the dial, and sine and cosine are its shadows on the two axes.
leaves.why: Linear Algebra already uses a bearing and a rotation matrix borrowed from here; the dial is the most draggable object in the tree.

leaves.name: Exponentials and logarithms
leaves.brief: Repeated multiplication grows fast, and the logarithm counts the steps.
leaves.sentence: Repeated multiplication grows or shrinks at a rate set by the base, and the logarithm asks how many steps it took.
leaves.why: Big-O, growth, entropy in bits, and the two towns' 0.7ⁿ decay all live here.

leaves.name: Logic and sets
leaves.brief: A statement is true or false, and a set is a collection with a membership test.
leaves.sentence: A statement is true or false, a set is a collection with a membership test, and the two are the same idea written two ways.
leaves.why: The vocabulary of every proof and every query; plates are toggles, truth tables and Venn regions. Reading and using logic only.

leaves.name: Counting
leaves.brief: Counting is choosing: does order matter, and are repeats allowed?
leaves.sentence: Counting is choosing, and the two questions are whether order matters and whether repeats are allowed.
leaves.why: Probability cannot start without it; keyspace sizes and the birthday bound are counting arguments with immediate bite for security students.

leaves.name: Modular arithmetic
leaves.brief: Arithmetic on the dial wraps round, and every question becomes where the dial lands.
leaves.sentence: Arithmetic on the dial wraps round, and the questions of inverses, primes and powers all become questions about where the dial lands.
leaves.why: The missing half of the Hill cipher branch; the floor for RSA and Diffie-Hellman; self-contained, so it is the second leaf to build.

leaves.name: Graphs
leaves.brief: A graph is dots joined by lines, and most questions ask which dots you can reach.
leaves.sentence: A graph is dots joined by lines, and almost every question about it is a question about which dots you can reach from which.
leaves.why: The adjacency matrix meets Linear Algebra page 6, and PageRank needs a graph before it needs an eigenvector.

leaves.name: Probability
leaves.brief: Probability is the share of the outcomes that count.
leaves.sentence: Probability is the share of the outcomes that count, and conditioning means changing which outcomes are in the room.
leaves.why: The two towns are a Markov chain, so this leaf and Linear Algebra page 18 describe one object from two sides.

leaves.name: Statistics and data
leaves.brief: A dataset is a cloud of points, and statistics are the few numbers that describe its shape.
leaves.sentence: A dataset is a cloud of points, and statistics are the few numbers that describe its shape.
leaves.why: Regression is the anchor Linear Algebra page 15 promises, and the covariance matrix is symmetric, so PCA becomes a branch off pages 19 and 20. This leaf's hatch fixes the fifteen's values.

leaves.name: Sequences, limits and series
leaves.brief: A sequence keeps going, and a limit is where it is heading.
leaves.sentence: A sequence is a rule that keeps going, and a limit is where it is heading even if it never arrives.
leaves.why: 0.7ⁿ settling, power iteration converging, the geometric series, and the floating-point moment where a limit computed in JS goes wrong.

leaves.name: Differentiation
leaves.brief: The derivative is the slope of the curve when you zoom in until it looks straight.
leaves.sentence: The derivative is the slope of the curve if you zoom in far enough for it to look straight.
leaves.why: The derivative is the best local linear machine, so this leaf and Linear Algebra page 6 are one thought at two scales.

leaves.name: Integration
leaves.brief: Integration adds up thin slices, and adding slices undoes taking slopes.
leaves.sentence: Integration adds up infinitely many thin slices, and the fundamental theorem says that adding slices undoes taking slopes.
leaves.why: Accumulation, area, and probability densities as areas, which closes a loop back to Probability.
